opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the standard we've been aiming for, and that I'd like us to keep hitting, is that each new Flash model should be about as good as, or better than, the previous generation's Pro model. So the Flash of generation N should roughly match or beat the Pro of generation N minus one, while staying much cheaper and much faster to serve.

That matters because Flash is the model that gets used at enormous scale. It's in a lot of products, it's what many developers build on, and latency and cost really matter there. If you can take the capabilities that were frontier a generation ago and deliver them at a fraction of the cost and with much lower latency, that unlocks a lot of new uses. Things that weren't economical before become very practical.

A lot of that comes from distillation. The bigger, more capable models act as teachers, and we can carry a surprising amount of their capability into a smaller, more efficient model. Then there are the hardware and systems improvements, the TPU work, and better inference techniques, which all add up.

So the bar is roughly: last generation's Pro-level quality at Flash-level speed and cost. And ideally we keep pushing so that the gap between the very best model and the one you can afford to run everywhere stays as small as possible.

r001.rationale: It says each new Flash model should be about as good as or better than the previous generation’s Pro model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing we've tried to hold ourselves to with Flash, and I think it's a pretty good North Star, is that each new Flash generation should roughly match the quality of the previous generation's Pro model. So the Flash model you get a generation later is about as good as the frontier model was a generation ago, but at a small fraction of the cost and latency.

I like that standard because it's concrete and it's demanding. It forces you to keep pushing on distillation, on architecture, on data quality, on training efficiency, on the serving side with TPUs and quantization and so on. You can't just make the small model a little better each time and call it progress. You have to close the gap to what was the state of the art not that long ago.

And the reason that matters is that cost and latency are what actually determine where these models get used. A lot of the most interesting applications aren't the ones where someone sits and waits twenty seconds for the best possible answer. They're the ones where the model is called a thousand times in a pipeline, or it's running on the fly inside a product that lots of people use every day, or it's in an agentic loop making many small decisions. For those, the question is really: how much intelligence can you get per dollar, and per millisecond? If Flash keeps riding that curve, you bring a frontier-level capability from a year or so ago to essentially everyone, and that's where the compounding benefit comes from.

So I'd want to keep that bar. And honestly, if we ever found we couldn't hit it, I'd take that as an interesting signal that we need to rethink something about how we're building these models rather than just lowering the target.

r001.rationale: The response says each new Flash generation should roughly match the quality of the previous generation’s Pro model.
